summary: A 1971 informational note by R. W. Watson describing an interactive network experiment to study modes of access to the Network Information Center.

eli5.summary: An experiment to see how people best use the network's information library.

questions: what was the network information center
how did early internet users interact with remote systems
subtitle: An early experiment on remote access to networked information systems

tldr.problem: Early 1970s researchers needed to understand how to make interactive systems usable over the network, especially with slow terminals and high latency.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 96 describes an experimental study to test different ways of accessing the Network Information Center over the network, comparing character-at-a-time and line-at-a-time communication modes, and different terminal speeds.
tldr.outcome: The experiment would provide data on which communication modes and access methods work best for interactive network use, informing the design of future networked systems.

today: RFC 96 is a historical record of how early ARPANET researchers approached the problem of interactive remote access. The lessons learned influenced the development of interactive network protocols and systems.

sections.title: The Interactive Network Experiment
sections.content:
RFC 96 describes a planned experiment to study how remote users can best interact with the Network Information Center (NIC) at Stanford Research Institute's Augmentation Research Center (SRI-ARC) over the network.

The NIC provided a full-featured online system (NLS, the "oN-Line System") designed for working with structured text. However, this system was originally built for local terminals with high-speed, full-duplex connections. The question was: how well would it work over the network with slow remote terminals and network delays?
sections.eli5: A library wanted to let people use its computer system from far away, but network delays could make it frustrating. They planned to test what works best.

sections.title: Three Access Modes
sections.content:
The experiment would test three different communication modes. In the simplest mode, the remote Telnet program sends each character to the NIC, which echoes it back. This fully mimics local use but creates the most network traffic and delays.

In a half-duplex mode, the remote system echoes characters locally and only sends complete commands to the NIC, reducing network traffic. A third approach would place a "front end" program at the remote site to handle more of the processing locally, reducing messages sent over the network.
sections.eli5: They would try three ways: send every letter, send full words, or have the remote computer help with some of the work to reduce network messages.

sections.title: Testing Different Terminal Speeds
sections.content:
The experiment would measure performance with terminal speeds of 10, 15, and 30 characters per second to understand how slow devices affected the experience. Response time statistics would be collected using existing monitoring facilities at both SRI and the cooperating remote site.

Rather than formal productivity studies, the experiment would gather subjective user feedback on which communication modes felt most comfortable to use despite network delays. This information would help guide how other organizations should implement network access to shared resources.
sections.eli5: They'd test with slow typing speeds and measure how long users had to wait for responses, then ask them which method felt best to use.

references.text: Watson, R. W., "NIC Access Conventions", NWG/RFC 97, 1971.
